papers.full_text: AbstractBackground: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) remain a major cause of hospitalization and mortality, particularly among children and other vulnerable populations. Early identification of pathogens and disease severity is essential for clinical decision-making. This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort.Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival. ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. ViVI scores reflect clinical severity at presentation, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity. Coinfections include viral-viral and viral-bacterial combinations detected by multiplex PCR and/or standard microbiological methods.HRSV: human respiratory syncytial virus; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ViVI Score: ViVI Disease Severity ScoreOrganism / CoinfectionMedian ViVI scoreIQR (interquartile range)Number of patientsType of infectionHuman respiratory syncytial viruses A/B20.513.538Single InfectionStaphylococcus aureus20195Single InfectionInfluenza B virus20.510.254Single InfectionStreptococcus pneumoniae296.53Single InfectionHuman rhinovirus3562Single InfectionHuman adenovirus3701Single InfectionHuman parainfluenza virus 44201Single InfectionHRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2113.7510CoinfectionHRSV + Human rhinovirus2043CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B virus32162CoinfectionHRSV + Staphylococcus aureus 2032CoinfectionAdenovirus + HRSV1601CoinfectionCoronavirus OC43 + HRSV1601CoinfectionMetapneumovirus + HRSV4501CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 3 + Parainfluenza virus 41101CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 4 + Parechovirus801CoinfectionRhinovirus + Staphylococcus aureus 2901CoinfectionInfluenza B virus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2901CoinfectionStaphylococcus aureus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 3501CoinfectionHRSV + Parainfluenza virus 41501CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B + Staphylococcus aureus 2701CoinfectionClinical outcomes and mortalityThe overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases.Predictive utility of the ViVI ScoreA total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3).Figure 3Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating the predictive performance of the ViVI Disease Severity Score for mortalityThe ROC plot displays the relationship between the false positive fraction (FPF: 1 − specificity) on the x-axis and the true positive fraction (TPF: sensitivity) on the y-axis across decision thresholds. The blue curve with red markers represents the binormal ROC curve fitted using maximum-likelihood estimation (JROCFIT), while the grey envelopes depict the 95% confidence interval around the fitted curve. The empirical (nonparametric) ROC operating points are shown as black markers (with the green connection, where applicable). Overall discrimination was excellent (fitted AUC ≈ 0.946; empirical AUC ≈ 0.942), with the curve lying close to the upper-left corner, indicating high sensitivity at low false-positive rates.The ROC curve lies close to the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discriminatory performance of the ViVI Score for predicting mortality across a range of decision thresholds (Figure 3). Using the ViVI Score as a mortality predictor and classifying death as the event, a low cutoff of ViVI ≥15 yielded 100% sensitivity for death (24/24) but low specificity (29.0%, 27/93) (TP=24, FN=0, TN=27, FP=66). In contrast, a high cutoff of ViVI ≥45 yielded 100% specificity (93/93) but low sensitivity (25.0%, 6/24) (TP=6, FN=18, TN=93, FP=0). The optimal threshold by Youden's J was ViVI ≥30, which provided balanced performance (sensitivity 83.3% (20/24) and specificity 91.4% (85/93); overall accuracy 89.7% (105/117)) (TP=20, FN=4, TN=85, FP=8). Patients with ViVI ≥30 had markedly increased odds of death compared with those with ViVI <30 (odds ratio 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; Fisher's exact test p=1.4 × 10−12). DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival.
full_text_sections.results: ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. The global burden of HRSV is substantial. A systematic analysis estimated 33.0 million HRSV-associated acute lower respiratory infection episodes, 3.6 million hospital admissions, and 101,400 deaths among children younger than five years in 2019, with the majority of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries [19].The frequency of co-infections observed in our cohort is also consistent with previous pediatric SARI studies using multiplex molecular platforms. Lamrani Hanchi et al. reported pathogen detection in 72.5% of hospitalized children and co-infection in 23.3%, highlighting the ability of multiplex PCR to identify multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen [20]. Similarly, studies incorporating digital surveillance and virological characterization have emphasized the value of combining pathogen detection with standardized clinical information [21,22]. These findings support the use of syndromic molecular testing as an adjunct to conventional microbiological investigations in patients with severe respiratory disease. However, detection of a respiratory pathogen does not necessarily establish causality, particularly for respiratory viruses that may be detected during prolonged shedding or asymptomatic infection. Therefore, multiplex PCR results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, disease severity, and conventional microbiological results.The exceptionally high mortality observed among SARI patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) was substantially higher than the overall mortality in the cohort. This finding is consistent with pediatric intensive-care data demonstrating significant mortality among children with bloodstream-infection-associated severe sepsis [23]. The finding emphasizes the importance of early recognition of bacterial superinfection and sepsis among patients presenting with severe respiratory illness, particularly when clinical deterioration or evidence of systemic infection is present.HRSV-associated disease severity is influenced by age and underlying clinical conditions. Recent multicenter pediatric data have demonstrated increased risk of severe RSV disease among younger children, premature infants, and older children with pulmonary or neurological, neuromuscular, or developmental conditions [24]. In our cohort, children with underlying hematological disorders represented an important high-risk subgroup, and HRSV-associated ARDS was associated with severe clinical outcomes. These findings reinforce the importance of identifying underlying risk factors when assessing patients with HRSV-associated SARI.The ViVI Score provided a structured approach to clinical severity assessment. Previous work has emphasized the importance of standardized severity assessment for respiratory viral illness and SARI [5]. More recent severity scales have also been evaluated to support respiratory hospitalization surveillance and viral genomic surveillance [25]. In our cohort, a ViVI score of ≥30 demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with an AUC of 0.946. This finding supports the potential utility of standardized severity assessment for identifying patients at increased risk of poor outcomes. However, prospective validation in independent populations is required before this threshold can be considered for broader clinical implementation.Raised PCT and CRP concentrations were associated with culture-positive sepsis and adverse clinical outcomes in our cohort. Previous pediatric data have evaluated PCT and CRP as markers of sepsis, with PCT potentially providing useful information regarding bacterial infection and disease severity [26]. However, neither biomarker should be interpreted as a stand-alone diagnostic test. Their value is greatest when interpreted together with the clinical presentation, microbiological findings, and other laboratory parameters.The findings also have implications for respiratory disease surveillance and clinical triage. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment can provide information on both pathogen circulation and clinical severity [21,22,25]. Such an approach may be particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings, where molecular diagnostic capacity is concentrated at tertiary-care facilities, and timely referral of patients with severe disease remains important. In primary-care settings, recognition of clinical warning signs and timely referral remain essential, while tertiary-care molecular testing can provide additional etiological information.The post-pandemic period is particularly relevant for respiratory pathogen surveillance because changes in population immunity, non-pharmaceutical interventions, and patterns of viral circulation may influence the timing and intensity of respiratory virus activity [16]. Continued surveillance is therefore important for identifying changing epidemiological patterns, detecting populations at increased risk of severe disease, and informing healthcare preparedness.The predominance of HRSV in our cohort also highlights the importance of preventive strategies. Current approaches to prevention of severe RSV disease include maternal vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibody strategies, particularly for infants at greatest risk of severe disease [27]. Continued pathogen-specific surveillance will be important for evaluating the epidemiological impact of these interventions.The study has several strengths. It integrates multiplex molecular diagnostics with conventional microbiological culture, inflammatory biomarkers, and standardized severity assessment, allowing simultaneous evaluation of pathogen distribution, bacterial superinfection, disease severity, and mortality. The use of a standardized severity score also enabled quantitative assessment of the relationship between clinical severity and mortality.In this study, several limitations should nevertheless be considered. The retrospective single-center design and relatively small sample size limit generalizability. The cohort was predominantly pediatric (103 children and 14 adults), which reflects the population evaluated at our center during the study period. Consequently, the findings, particularly those related to pathogen distribution, disease severity, and mortality risk stratification, should be interpreted primarily in the context of pediatric SARI and may not be directly generalizable to adult SARI populations. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsHRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen identified among hospitalized patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI. Multiplex molecular testing provided useful etiological information, while the ViVI Score demonstrated good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort. Further prospective studies in larger and more diverse populations are needed to validate these findings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSevere acute respiratory infections (SARI) pose a significant global health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines SARI as an acute respiratory illness with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization [1]. However, this syndromic definition does not provide information regarding the underlying etiological agent or the individual risk of adverse outcomes. SARI may result from a wide range of viral and bacterial pathogens, and conventional diagnostic methods may not always provide a timely or comprehensive etiological diagnosis.Before the COVID-19 pandemic, SARI detection was largely syndromic, relying on clinical presentation and limited diagnostic capacity [2]. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for strengthening surveillance systems and pathogen identification. In India, surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases is supported through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, including laboratory-based and information technology-enabled surveillance [3].SARI constitutes a major cause of healthcare utilization and hospitalization and may require referral to secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, particularly among young children, older adults, and individuals with underlying comorbidities. Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2].In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4].To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison.The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7].Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings. papers.title_original: Molecular Etiology and Mortality Risk Stratification of Non-SARS-CoV-2 Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in a Predominantly Pediatric Cohort: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens responsible for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a predominantly pediatric cohort, addressing the need for better diagnostic tools in resource-limited settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in North India from September to December 2021, analyzing 117 patients admitted with SARI during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.methods: Multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture were used to detect respiratory pathogens. The study cohort comprised 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection was performed using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus assay, and statistical analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test.
analysis.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the predominant pathogen. A cutoff of ≥30 in the ViVI Score yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity, strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, and bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. The ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with a cutoff of ≥30 showing strong association.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the ViVI Score can be a useful tool for clinical triage and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings, and HRSV is a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the small sample size, which may affect generalizability. The high mortality rate in patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) highlights the need for better diagnostic and treatment strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This study identified HRSV as the predominant respiratory pathogen in a cohort of 117 pediatric and adult patients with severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in North India. The ViVI Score, with a cutoff of ≥30, showed strong association with mortality (OR 53.1, p<0.001), suggesting its utility in clinical triage and surveillance.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens responsible for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a predominantly pediatric cohort, addressing the need for better diagnostic tools in resource-limited settings.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in North India from September to December 2021, analyzing 117 patients admitted with SARI during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis_en.methods: Multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture were used to detect respiratory pathogens. The study cohort comprised 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection was performed using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus assay, and statistical analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test.
analysis_en.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the predominant pathogen. A cutoff of ≥30 in the ViVI Score yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity, strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, and bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. The ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with a cutoff of ≥30 showing strong association.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the ViVI Score can be a useful tool for clinical triage and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings, and HRSV is a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in children.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the small sample size, which may affect generalizability. The high mortality rate in patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) highlights the need for better diagnostic and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Clesrovimab in the new era of RSV prevention: one season, one dose, one chance.
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization in infancy worldwide. Historically, prevention relied on monthly palivizumab administration for selected high-risk infants, despite evidence that a substantial proportion of severe RSV disease occurs in previously healthy term infants. The recent introduction of maternal RSV vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibodies has transformed the prevention landscape. Clesrovimab (MK-1654; Enflonsia) is a long-acting monoclonal antibody designed to provide season-long protection following a single dose. In the pivotal phase 2b/3 CLEVER trial, clesrovimab reduced RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization among infants entering their first RSV season, with a safety profile comparable to placebo. The absolute risk reduction for RSV hospitalization was approximately 1.9 percentage points, corresponding to an estimated number needed to treat of 51 infants over 150 days of follow-up. In this policy-focused clinical perspective informed by a narrative review, we examine the emerging role of clesrovimab within contemporary RSV prevention strategies. We discuss efficacy, safety, implementation challenges, economic considerations, and remaining evidence gaps, including the absence of head-to-head comparisons with nirsevimab, limited post-licensure data, and uncertainties regarding long-term effectiveness and affordability. Future success will depend not only on efficacy but also on equitable access, sustainable implementation, and ongoing surveillance. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The emergence of long-acting monoclonal antibodies has expanded preventive options for infants at risk of RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease during their first RSV season. For clinicians, the key shift is that RSV prevention is increasingly being considered within a broader population-health framework rather than solely as a risk-based intervention for selected high-risk groups. Clesrovimab, alongside nirsevimab and maternal RSV vaccination, represents one component of an evolving prevention strategy aimed at reducing RSV-associated morbidity and hospitalization during early infancy. From a practical perspective, successful implementation will depend on timely administration, integration into neonatal discharge planning and well-child care pathways, and coordination with maternal immunization programs. As RSV prevention moves into routine clinical practice, equitable access, sustained coverage, affordability, and ongoing post-licensure surveillance will be as important as efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials. Ultimately, the greatest reductions in RSV-related hospitalization are likely to result from effective delivery of preventive strategies to the infants at highest risk during the RSV season. KEY POINTS: RSV continues to impose a substantial burden on infants worldwide despite decades of clinical recognition and supportive care. Most RSV hospitalizations occur in infants without traditional high-risk conditions, highlighting the limitations of selective prophylaxis strategies. Long-acting monoclonal antibodies and maternal RSV vaccination have transformed prevention from a niche intervention into a population-level public health strategy. Clesrovimab demonstrated significant protection against RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization in healthy infants entering their first RSV season. Future research should focus on comparative effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, long-term safety, implementation in low-resource settings, and optimization of delivery strategies to maximize population impact.

papers.title_zh: RSV 预防新时代的 Clesrovimab:一个季节、一剂、一次机会。
papers.source_body_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization in infancy worldwide. Historically, prevention relied on monthly palivizumab administration for selected high-risk infants, despite evidence that a substantial proportion of severe RSV disease occurs in previously healthy term infants. The recent introduction of maternal RSV vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibodies has transformed the prevention landscape. Clesrovimab (MK-1654; Enflonsia) is a long-acting monoclonal antibody designed to provide season-long protection following a single dose. In the pivotal phase 2b/3 CLEVER trial, clesrovimab reduced RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization among infants entering their first RSV season, with a safety profile comparable to placebo. The absolute risk reduction for RSV hospitalization was approximately 1.9 percentage points, corresponding to an estimated number needed to treat of 51 infants over 150 days of follow-up. In this policy-focused clinical perspective informed by a narrative review, we examine the emerging role of clesrovimab within contemporary RSV prevention strategies. We discuss efficacy, safety, implementation challenges, economic considerations, and remaining evidence gaps, including the absence of head-to-head comparisons with nirsevimab, limited post-licensure data, and uncertainties regarding long-term effectiveness and affordability. Future success will depend not only on efficacy but also on equitable access, sustainable implementation, and ongoing surveillance. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The emergence of long-acting monoclonal antibodies has expanded preventive options for infants at risk of RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease during their first RSV season. For clinicians, the key shift is that RSV prevention is increasingly being considered within a broader population-health framework rather than solely as a risk-based intervention for selected high-risk groups. Clesrovimab, alongside nirsevimab and maternal RSV vaccination, represents one component of an evolving prevention strategy aimed at reducing RSV-associated morbidity and hospitalization during early infancy. From a practical perspective, successful implementation will depend on timely administration, integration into neonatal discharge planning and well-child care pathways, and coordination with maternal immunization programs. As RSV prevention moves into routine clinical practice, equitable access, sustained coverage, affordability, and ongoing post-licensure surveillance will be as important as efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials. Ultimately, the greatest reductions in RSV-related hospitalization are likely to result from effective delivery of preventive strategies to the infants at highest risk during the RSV season. KEY POINTS: RSV continues to impose a substantial burden on infants worldwide despite decades of clinical recognition and supportive care. Most RSV hospitalizations occur in infants without traditional high-risk conditions, highlighting the limitations of selective prophylaxis strategies. Long-acting monoclonal antibodies and maternal RSV vaccination have transformed prevention from a niche intervention into a population-level public health strategy. Clesrovimab demonstrated significant protection against RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalization in healthy infants entering their first RSV season. Future research should focus on comparative effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, long-term safety, implementation in low-resource settings, and optimization of delivery strategies to maximize population impact.

papers.title: Cost‐effectiveness analysis of the mRNA‐1345 RSV vaccine for older adults in Italy.
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an important cause of respiratory disease in older adults and adults with chronic medical conditions, contributing substantially to the healthcare burden in Italy. The availability of effective RSV vaccines provides an opportunity to reduce RSV-related morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs in populations at high risk of severe disease. This study evaluates the potential public health impact and cost-effectiveness of vaccination using mRNA-1345 administered as a single dose compared with no vaccination in Italian high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years. Methods A static decision-analytic model was developed to project clinical and economic outcomes over a 5-year time horizon. Economic outcomes were evaluated from the Italian National Health Service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, SSN) perspective. Model inputs were informed by the most recent Italian epidemiological, clinical, and economic evidence, supplemented by published international data when necessary. Deterministic, probabilistic, and scenario analyses were conducted to assess the impact of uncertainty in model inputs and assumptions on the study results. Results Vaccination with mRNA-1345 in high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years was projected to avert over 19,800 hospitalizations, 4,000 emergency department visits, 381,000 outpatient visits, 6,000 RSV-attributable deaths, and 212,000 antibiotic prescriptions compared with no vaccination over a 5-year period. The total incremental cost of €1,143 million and the additional 47,477 QALYs gained resulted in an ICER of €24,078, which was below the commonly referenced willingness to-pay range of €33,000- 40,000 per QALY gained. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of the analysis results. Conclusions Vaccination with mRNA-1345 is a cost-effective strategy for the prevention of RSV in high- risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults ≥75 years in Italy and has the potential to provide substantial public health benefits. Key Summary Points Why carry out this study? The clinical and economic burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in high-risk and older adults is significant. RSV vaccines have received regulatory authorization in Europe, and national recommendations or immunization programs for older adults have been introduced in several countries including Germany, France, Spain and the United Kingdom. source_records.title: Cost‐effectiveness analysis of the mRNA‐1345 RSV vaccine for older adults in Italy.
source_records.abstract: AIMS: To evaluate the potential public health impact and cost-effectiveness of vaccination using mRNA-1345 administered as a single dose compared with no vaccination in Italian high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years. METHODS: A static decision-analytic model was developed to project clinical and economic outcomes over a five-year time horizon, assuming 50% vaccination coverage among eligible adults. Economic outcomes were evaluated from the Italian National Health Service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, SSN) perspective. Model inputs were informed by the most recent Italian epidemiological, clinical, and economic evidence, supplemented by published international data when necessary. Deterministic, probabilistic, and scenario analyses were conducted to assess the impact of uncertainty in model inputs and assumptions on the study results. RESULTS: Vaccination with mRNA-1345 in high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years was projected to avert over 19,800 hospitalizations, 4,000 emergency department visits, 381,000 outpatient visits, 6,000 RSV-attributable deaths, and 212,000 antibiotic prescriptions compared with no vaccination over a five-year period. The total incremental cost of €1,143 million and the additional 47,477 QALYs gained resulted in an ICER of €24,078 per QALY gained, which was below the commonly referenced willingness-to-pay range of €33,000-40,000/QALY. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of the analysis results. LIMITATIONS: Due to limited epidemiological evidence for Italy, selected epidemiological inputs were informed by studies conducted in other high-income countries. In addition, vaccine efficacy beyond the two-year clinical trial follow-up was projected to five years using nonlinear waning curves fitted to the observed trial data. CONCLUSIONS: Vaccination with mRNA-1345 is a cost-effective strategy for the prevention of RSV in high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults ≥75 years in Italy, in comparison to no vaccination, and has the potential to provide substantial public health benefits.

In Italy, RSV vaccination for older adults has not yet been implemented as a uniform national program, however such a program has been endorsed by several scientific societies. The study objective was to estimate the potential public health impact and cost- effectiveness of vaccination using mRNA-1345 administered as a single dose compared with no vaccination in Italian high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years, in the 5-year period following vaccination. What was learned from the study? Vaccination of high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years with mRNA- 1345 was projected to prevent more than 19,800 hospitalizations, 4,000 ED visits, 381,000 outpatient visits, 6,000 RSV-attributable deaths, and 212,000 antibiotic prescriptions (up to 21% reduction across outcomes), in comparison to no vaccination, over a 5-year period. This analysis suggests the mRNA-1345 vaccine is a cost-effective strategy for the prevention of RSV in high-risk adults in Italy and has the potential for substantial public health benefit. Our findings provide evidence to inform national immunization policy and reimbursement decisions, and support the implementation of an RSV vaccination program for high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years in Italy. Plain Language Summary Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common virus that causes lung infections. It can be especially dangerous for older adults and people with health conditions like asthma, heart disease, or diabetes. Each year, RSV causes many hospitalizations and deaths in Italy. A new vaccine called mRNA-1345 was recently approved to protect individuals aged 18 years and older against severe RSV disease. This study looked at whether vaccinating the most vulnerable adults, particularly people aged 60-74 years with chronic health conditions and everyone aged 75 years and older, would help reduce the burden of RSV and provide good value for money for the healthcare system. Researchers used a mathematical model to compare what might happen over 5 years with and without vaccination. They found that using a single-dose vaccination strategy could prevent over 19,800 hospitalizations and more than 6,000 deaths over the following 5 years. Although vaccination requires investments, the health benefits are estimated to be large enough for mRNA-1345 to provide good value for money for the Italian healthcare system.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估 mRNA-1345 RSV 疫苗 在降低意大利高危老年人 RSV 相关发病率、死亡率 和医疗费用方面的潜在公共卫生影响和成本效益。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 开发了静态决策分析模型,用于预测 60-74 岁意大利高危成年人和所有 75 岁以上成年人 5 年时间范围内的临床和经济结果。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究使用数学模型来比较单剂量 疫苗接种 策略与无 疫苗接种 策略的结果,并结合了来自意大利和国际来源的流行病学、临床和经济数据。
analysis_zh.main_results: 与未使用 疫苗接种 的 5 年相比,使用 mRNA-1345 的 疫苗接种 预计可避免超过 19,800 例住院治疗、4,000 例急诊就诊、381,000 例门诊就诊、6,000 例 RSV 所致死亡以及 212,000 份抗生素处方。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,mRNA-1345 疫苗 可以通过减少高危成年人的 RSV 负担来提供实质性的公共健康益处,其 ICER 为 24,078 欧元,低于通常提到的每获得 QALY 33,000-40,000 欧元的支付意愿范围。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,针对意大利 60-74 岁高危成年人和所有 75 岁以上成年人实施 RSV 疫苗接种 计划可以显着减轻医疗负担并提供良好的经济效益。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于静态模型,并依赖于对 疫苗 的有效性和成本的假设,这可能会影响结果的稳健性。

papers.title: RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 in hospitalized children: A comparative analysis of the 2025/2026 epidemic season in Poland.
papers.abstract: Comparative data on the epidemiology and clinical impact of RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 infections among hospitalized children during the same epidemic season remain limited in Central Europe. This multicenter retrospective study compared the epidemiological characteristics, clinical presentations, and outcomes of laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and COVID-19 among hospitalized children in Poland during. A total of 756 patients were evaluated, including 408 with influenza (54.0%), 204 with COVID-19 (27.0%), and 144 with RSV (19.0%). The infections displayed distinct temporal patterns, peaking sequentially from early autumn (COVID-19) through winter (influenza) and early spring (RSV). Demographically, hospitalizations for RSV infection and COVID-19 skewed toward infants and young children (mean ages 1.8 and 2.3 years, respectively), whereas influenza affected a broader age spectrum, extending into (pre)school-aged cohorts (mean age 4.5 years; p < 0.0001). RSV infection was associated with the highest requirement for oxygen support (41.7%) and the longest hospital stay (mean, 6.0 days) compared with influenza and COVID-19 (p < 0.0001). Conversely, pneumonia was most frequently diagnosed in the COVID-19 group (16.2%; p = 0.01), which also exhibited unique elevations in D-dimer levels (p = 0.02). Vaccine and immunoprophylaxis uptake hovered near zero across all cohorts (∼1%). Empirical antibiotic use was highly prevalent (26.6%), exceeding objective pneumonia rates by two-to three-fold. Major pediatric respiratory viruses maintain unique clinical and demographic footprints. The observed low immunization rates and disproportionate antibiotic use underscore an urgent need for targeted pediatric vaccination campaigns and antimicrobial stewardship programs.

papers.title_zh: 住院儿童中的 RSV、流感和 COVID-19:波兰 2025/2026 年流行季的比较分析。
papers.source_body_en: Comparative data on the epidemiology and clinical impact of RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 infections among hospitalized children during the same epidemic season remain limited in Central Europe. This multicenter retrospective study compared the epidemiological characteristics, clinical presentations, and outcomes of laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and COVID-19 among hospitalized children in Poland during. A total of 756 patients were evaluated, including 408 with influenza (54.0%), 204 with COVID-19 (27.0%), and 144 with RSV (19.0%). The infections displayed distinct temporal patterns, peaking sequentially from early autumn (COVID-19) through winter (influenza) and early spring (RSV). Demographically, hospitalizations for RSV infection and COVID-19 skewed toward infants and young children (mean ages 1.8 and 2.3 years, respectively), whereas influenza affected a broader age spectrum, extending into (pre)school-aged cohorts (mean age 4.5 years; p < 0.0001). RSV infection was associated with the highest requirement for oxygen support (41.7%) and the longest hospital stay (mean, 6.0 days) compared with influenza and COVID-19 (p < 0.0001). Conversely, pneumonia was most frequently diagnosed in the COVID-19 group (16.2%; p = 0.01), which also exhibited unique elevations in D-dimer levels (p = 0.02). Vaccine and immunoprophylaxis uptake hovered near zero across all cohorts (∼1%). Empirical antibiotic use was highly prevalent (26.6%), exceeding objective pneumonia rates by two-to three-fold. Major pediatric respiratory viruses maintain unique clinical and demographic footprints. The observed low immunization rates and disproportionate antibiotic use underscore an urgent need for targeted pediatric vaccination campaigns and antimicrobial stewardship programs.
papers.abstract_zh: 在中欧,关于同一流行季节住院儿童中 RSV、流感和 SARS-CoV-2 感染的 流行病学 和临床影响的比较数据仍然有限。这项多中心回顾性研究比较了波兰住院儿童中实验室确诊的 呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV)、流感和 COVID-19 的流行病学特征、临床表现和结果。共有 756 名患者接受了评估,其中 408 名流感患者(54.0%)、204 名 COVID-19 患者(27.0%)和 144 名 RSV 患者(19.0%)。感染表现出不同的时间模式,从初秋(COVID-19)到冬季(流感)和早春(RSV)依次达到高峰。从人口统计学角度来看,因 RSV 感染和 COVID-19 住院的患者多为婴儿和幼儿(平均年龄分别为 1.8 岁和 2.3 岁),而流感影响的年龄范围更广,延伸至学龄前 队列研究(平均年龄 4.5 岁;p < 0.0001)。与流感和 COVID-19 相比,RSV 感染与最高的氧气支持需求 (41.7%) 和最长的住院时间(平均 6.0 天)相关 (p < 0.0001)。相反,肺炎在 COVID-19 组中最常被诊断出来(16.2%;p = 0.01),该组的 D-二聚体水平也表现出独特的升高(p = 0.02)。所有 疫苗 和免疫预防的吸收率徘徊在零附近(∼1%)。经验性抗生素使用非常普遍(26.6%),比客观肺炎发生率高出两到三倍。主要的儿科呼吸道病毒保持着独特的临床和人口特征。观察到的低免疫率和不成比例的抗生素使用强调迫切需要有针对性的儿科 疫苗接种 运动和抗菌药物管理计划。

papers.title: The socioeconomic value of adult respiratory vaccination in Australia: a benefit-cost analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pneumococcal disease, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza and COVID-19 cause a major burden of illness and death among adults, much of which is vaccine-preventable. We estimated the societal value of adult vaccination against these four pathogens in Australia. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: We developed disease-specific static life table cohort models and conducted a societal-perspective benefit-cost analysis of adult respiratory vaccination, approximating those recommended by the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunization, relative to no vaccination. Mortality risk reductions were monetized using value of a statistical life (VSL) and value of a statistical life year (VSLY); avoided morbidity and productivity losses were also captured. Main outcomes were benefit-cost ratios (BCRs) and net monetary benefits (NMBs). RESULTS: Over ten years, age and risk-based vaccination generated gross returns of $11.24 (VSL) and $5.69 (VSLY) per Australian dollar invested (net returns $10.24 and $4.69), with NMBs of $64.97 billion and $29.76 billion, averting 234,187 hospitalizations and 13,890 deaths. BCRs remained well above 1 across all scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: Adult respiratory vaccination shows strong societal returns. Improving coverage and extending eligibility offer the potential for further societal gains. Some simplifications in the model are likely to understate the value of vaccination while others may overstate it.

source_records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pneumococcal disease, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza and COVID-19 cause a major burden of illness and death among adults, much of which is vaccine-preventable. We estimated the societal value of adult vaccination against these four pathogens in Australia. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: We developed disease-specific static life table cohort models and conducted a societal-perspective benefit-cost analysis of adult respiratory vaccination, approximating those recommended by the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunization, relative to no vaccination. Mortality risk reductions were monetized using value of a statistical life (VSL) and value of a statistical life year (VSLY); avoided morbidity and productivity losses were also captured. Main outcomes were benefit-cost ratios (BCRs) and net monetary benefits (NMBs). RESULTS: Over ten years, age and risk-based vaccination generated gross returns of $11.24 (VSL) and $5.69 (VSLY) per Australian dollar invested (net returns $10.24 and $4.69), with NMBs of $64.97 billion and $29.76 billion, averting 234,187 hospitalizations and 13,890 deaths. BCRs remained well above 1 across all scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: Adult respiratory vaccination shows strong societal returns. Improving coverage and extending eligibility offer the potential for further societal gains. Some simplifications in the model are likely to understate the value of vaccination while others may overstate it.

The research employs a societal-perspective benefit-cost analysis using static life table cohort models to estimate the returns of vaccination programs. The evidence is presented with high confidence due to its focus on societal benefits and the use of established economic metrics.

papers.title: Nirsevimab provides age-specific protection against RSV hospitalisation in the first year of life: a population-level study in Queensland, Australia.
papers.abstract: Nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody with activity against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), was introduced into the Queensland paediatric RSV prevention program in 2024. Using Queensland Notifiable Conditions Register (NoCS) data, we found that the infant cohort eligible for the nirsevimab program had lower RSV hospitalisation rates than comparable pre-program cohorts. The population-level impact of nirsevimab was greatest during the first month of life (incidence rate ratio [IRR]: 0.22; 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.16-0.31; representing a 78% reduction in hospitalisation rate), with its magnitude gradually declining thereafter until nine months of age (IRR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.62-0.96; a 23% reduction), following which the impact of nirsevimab on hospitalisation rate, with increasing age of the infant or child, was no longer statistically significant. An interrupted time-series analysis demonstrated an immediate 63% reduction in RSV hospitalisations following nirsevimab's introduction (IRR: 0.37; 95% CI: 0.23-0.60), showing a substantial population-level impact of the program in Queensland, Australia.

The population-level impact of nirsevimab was greatest during the first month of life (incidence rate ratio [IRR]: 0.22; 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.16–0.31; representing a 78% reduction in hospitalisation rate), with its magnitude gradually declining thereafter until nine months of age (IRR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.62–0.96; a 23% reduction), following which the impact of nirsevimab on hospitalisation rate, with increasing age of the infant or child, was no longer statistically significant. An interrupted time-series analysis demonstrated an immediate 63% reduction in RSV hospitalisations following nirsevimab’s introduction (IRR: 0.37; 95% CI: 0.23–0.60), showing a substantial population-level impact of the program in Queensland, Australia.

papers.title: Nationwide survey of testing practices for respiratory viruses in Australia in the post COVID-19 pandemic era.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the wake of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, there have been dramatic changes in the testing protocols for respiratory illness. Laboratory identification of respiratory pathogens causing clinical symptoms has become more important in the post-COVID-19 era, both for epidemiological and clinical reasons. This is particularly the case for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where a number of preventatives are at the point of clinical translation. The laboratory diagnosis is one of the critical elements in understanding the disease burden of respiratory pathogens and the effectiveness of preventatives. The aims of this study were to understand current laboratory testing and reporting practices across Australia. METHODS: We undertook a cross-sectional survey of Australian NATA (National Association of Testing Authorities) accredited laboratories to collect data on patterns of laboratory testing, the methods used and their reporting processes. The survey asked participants to report on testing of respiratory samples for 2022 as well as current respiratory multiplex testing in 2023. OUTCOMES: In total, 45 out of 193 eligible laboratories (23%) completed the online survey. The majority of laboratories were from Victoria and New South Wales (31% and 27%, respectively) and most were hospital-based clinical diagnostic laboratories. Overall, 40% of responding laboratories (18/44) reported that > 80% of all tests in the molecular laboratory in 2023 were respiratory multiplex. Influenza viruses, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 were tested most frequently on respiratory multiplex PCR panels. RSV typing (RSV A or RSV B) was included in under a quarter of panels (9/43; 21%), compared to almost two-thirds for influenza typing (influenza A or influenza B: 29/44; 66%). There was considerable variability in testing platforms used, with thirty-seven laboratories using 87 different platforms (18 unique platforms). GeneXpert® (Cepheid) was the most commonly used platform; with a higher concentration of this instrument in laboratories from the eastern states (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria). Forty percent of laboratories reported changes to respiratory testing procedures/panels in 2023 compared to the previous year. Laboratories were most likely to report results directly to the referring doctor (96-100%) followed by notifying their jurisdictional Department of Health.

papers.title_zh: COVID-19 大流行后时代澳大利亚呼吸道病毒检测实践的全国调查。
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: In the wake of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, there have been dramatic changes in the testing protocols for respiratory illness. Laboratory identification of respiratory pathogens causing clinical symptoms has become more important in the post-COVID-19 era, both for epidemiological and clinical reasons. This is particularly the case for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where a number of preventatives are at the point of clinical translation. The laboratory diagnosis is one of the critical elements in understanding the disease burden of respiratory pathogens and the effectiveness of preventatives. The aims of this study were to understand current laboratory testing and reporting practices across Australia. METHODS: We undertook a cross-sectional survey of Australian NATA (National Association of Testing Authorities) accredited laboratories to collect data on patterns of laboratory testing, the methods used and their reporting processes. The survey asked participants to report on testing of respiratory samples for 2022 as well as current respiratory multiplex testing in 2023. OUTCOMES: In total, 45 out of 193 eligible laboratories (23%) completed the online survey. The majority of laboratories were from Victoria and New South Wales (31% and 27%, respectively) and most were hospital-based clinical diagnostic laboratories. Overall, 40% of responding laboratories (18/44) reported that > 80% of all tests in the molecular laboratory in 2023 were respiratory multiplex. Influenza viruses, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 were tested most frequently on respiratory multiplex PCR panels. RSV typing (RSV A or RSV B) was included in under a quarter of panels (9/43; 21%), compared to almost two-thirds for influenza typing (influenza A or influenza B: 29/44; 66%). There was considerable variability in testing platforms used, with thirty-seven laboratories using 87 different platforms (18 unique platforms). GeneXpert® (Cepheid) was the most commonly used platform; with a higher concentration of this instrument in laboratories from the eastern states (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria). Forty percent of laboratories reported changes to respiratory testing procedures/panels in 2023 compared to the previous year. Laboratories were most likely to report results directly to the referring doctor (96-100%) followed by notifying their jurisdictional Department of Health.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:2019 年冠状病毒病 (COVID-19) 大流行后,呼吸道疾病的检测方案发生了巨大变化。出于流行病学和临床原因,在后 COVID-19 时代,引起临床症状的呼吸道病原体的实验室鉴定变得更加重要。呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 的情况尤其如此,其中许多预防措施正处于临床转化阶段。诊断 实验室是了解呼吸道病原体的疾病负担和预防措施有效性的关键要素之一。这项研究的目的是了解澳大利亚当前的实验室检测和报告实践。方法:我们对澳大利亚 NATA(国家测试机构协会)认可的实验室进行了横断面调查,收集有关实验室测试模式、所用方法及其报告流程的数据。该调查要求参与者报告 2022 年呼吸道样本检测情况以及 2023 年当前呼吸道多重检测情况。结果:总共 193 个合格实验室中有 45 个 (23%) 完成了在线调查。大多数实验室来自维多利亚州和新南威尔士州(分别为 31% 和 27%),并且大多数是医院临床诊断实验室。总体而言,40% 的响应实验室 (18/44) 报告称,2023 年分子实验室所有测试中 80% 以上是呼吸多重测试。流感病毒、RSV 和 SARS-CoV-2 在呼吸道多重 PCR 检测板上最常进行测试。RSV 分型(RSV A 或 RSV B)包含在不到四分之一的小组中(9/43;21%),而流感分型则几乎占三分之二(甲型流感或乙型流感:29/44;66%)。所使用的测试平台存在相当大的差异,有 37 个实验室使用 87 个不同的平台(18 个独特的平台)。GeneXpert® (Cepheid) 是最常用的平台;该仪器在东部各州(新南威尔士州、昆士兰州、维多利亚州)的实验室中使用率较高。40% 的实验室报告称,与上一年相比,2023 年呼吸检测程序/面板发生了变化。实验室最有可能直接向转诊医生报告结果(96-100%),然后通知其管辖的卫生部。

papers.title: Molecular detection of respiratory viruses from breath samples: Evaluation of nucleic acid extraction systems and PCR panels
papers.abstract: Background: Reliable and scalable molecular testing is essential for risk assessment and monitoring of respiratory viruses with epidemic or pandemic potential. The AveloMask Kit (Avelo) is a non-invasive sampling device that collects exhaled breath aerosols (XBA) using a high-performance filter, which can be released into a stabilizing buffer for nucleic acid preservation. Detection of viral nucleic acids in breath samples remains challenging, as viral loads are typically lower than in conventional upper-respiratory swabs. Therefore, optimizing extraction and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) workflows is critical to maximizing analytical sensitivity. Methods In this proof-of-concept study, we compared the nucleic acid extraction efficiency of ELITe InGenius® (ELITech) and QIAsymphony (Qiagen) automated platforms in combination with an in-house real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) panel and a commercial PCR panel (RespiFinder® 2Smart, Pathofinder). Using synthetic ribonucleic acid (RNA) standards, we determined the limit of detection (LOD) for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as a performance indicator for both extraction platforms and PCR panels. As proof-of-concept, we analyzed seven XBA samples from infected individuals, eight from healthy controls, and one from a person recovering from a cold. Results Our results demonstrate that ELITe InGenius and QIAsymphony provide comparable extraction efficiencies without negatively impacting downstream RT-qPCR. The combination of QIAsymphony and RespiFinder 2Smart achieved LODs below 100 viral copies/mL and detected all pathogens in clinical XBA samples (7/7) that were also detected in matched swabs. Conclusions These initial findings suggest the compatibility of high-throughput extraction systems and PCR panels with XBA samples collected using AveloMask and warrant further investigation of XBA sampling as a non-invasive method for respiratory virus detection.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:可靠且可扩展的分子检测对于具有流行或大流行潜力的呼吸道病毒的风险评估和监测至关重要。AveloMask 套件 (Avelo) 是一种非侵入式采样设备,使用高性能过滤器收集呼出气溶胶 (XBA),可将其释放到稳定缓冲液中用于核酸保存。检测呼吸样本中的病毒核酸仍然具有挑战性,因为病毒载量通常低于传统上呼吸道拭子中的病毒载量。因此,优化提取和聚合酶链反应 (PCR) 工作流程对于最大化分析灵敏度至关重要。方法 在这项概念验证研究中,我们比较了 ELITe InGenius® (ELITech) 和 QIAsymphony (Qiagen) 自动化平台与内部实时定量聚合酶链反应 (RT-qPCR) 面板和商业 PCR 面板(RespiFinder® 2Smart、Pathofinder)相结合的核酸提取效率。使用合成核糖核酸 (RNA) 标准品,我们确定了严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒 2 (SARS-CoV-2)、甲型流感、乙型流感和 呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 的检测限 (LOD),作为提取平台和 PCR 组合的性能指标。作为概念验证,我们分析了来自感染者的 7 个 XBA 样本、8 个来自健康对照者的样本以及 1 个来自感冒康复者的样本。结果 我们的结果表明,ELITe InGenius 和 QIAsymphony 提供了相当的提取效率,且不会对下游 RT-qPCR 产生负面影响。QIAsymphony 和 RespiFinder 2Smart 的组合实现了低于 100 个病毒拷贝/mL 的 LOD,并检测到了临床 XBA 样本 (7/7) 中的所有病原体,这些病原体也在匹配的拭子中检测到。结论 这些初步研究结果表明,高通量提取系统和 PCR 检测板与使用 AveloMask 收集的 XBA 样本具有兼容性,并值得进一步研究 XBA 采样作为呼吸道病毒检测的非侵入性方法。
