A retrospective period-comparison study analyzed 230,333 patient-period records representing 197,630 children tested from January 2018 through December 2023. After strict pandemic controls, influenza A and M. pneumoniae rose above pre-pandemic positivity, while RSV increased chiefly among younger children and influenza B rebounded mainly in adolescents. The results describe test positivity among hospital attendees, not community incidence, and the researchers emphasized that changing testing practices and clinical case mix complicate direct comparisons. The investigators divided the six-year observation window into four periods: a pre-pandemic baseline from January 2018 through January 2020; Pandemic-I, from February 2020 through June 2021, when Guangzhou used stringent measures including lockdowns, school closures, masking and travel restrictions; Pandemic-II, from July 2021 through November 2022, when restrictions were relaxed and intermittent Omicron outbreaks occurred; and a post-pandemic period from December 2022 through December 2023, after full reopening. They tested associations using multivariable logistic regression, comparing positivity in each later period with the pre-pandemic baseline while adjusting for age, sex, inpatient or outpatient status and hospital campus. Age-period interactions were evaluated with robust Wald tests, and analyses were repeated in some form to assess the influence of repeated observations and changing denominators. Most respiratory viruses were detected less often during Pandemic-I, but the suppression was neither universal nor equally durable. Influenza A positivity fell from 19.2% before the pandemic to 5.0% during Pandemic-I, and influenza B declined from 6.5% to 0.5%. RSV fell from 21.8% to 12.3%, adenovirus from 18.4% to 1.1%, and M. pneumoniae from 12.4% to 2.2%. Rhinovirus, cytomegalovirus and bocavirus were notable exceptions to the broader viral decline. When controls were relaxed, influenza A positivity rose to 25.0%, already above its baseline, and reached 29.7% after reopening. M. pneumoniae increased more slowly, reaching 7.4% during Pandemic-II before surging to 24.1% in the post-pandemic period, the highest rate recorded for that pathogen across the four periods. Discover more Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering careers guide Bioengineering news subscription Bioengineering Career Guide Adjustment for the changing clinical population sharpened the principal contrasts. Relative to pre-pandemic levels, influenza A had an adjusted odds ratio of 0.23 during Pandemic-I, 1.26 during Pandemic-II and 1.52 after reopening. M. pneumoniae remained below baseline during Pandemic-II, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.54, but reached 1.99 after reopening despite a 9.3-fold expansion in the number tested. RSV produced a particularly instructive result: its crude post-pandemic positivity rate of 12.8% remained below the 21.8% baseline, yet its adjusted odds ratio was 1.31, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.06 to 1.63. Comparable-denominator analyses retained the post-pandemic increases for RSV, influenza A and M. pneumoniae, indicating that expanding testing alone did not fully account for the changes. Age-stratified models showed that these pathogen-level averages concealed substantial differences between younger and older children. RSV positivity after reopening was elevated among children aged 29 days to 23 months, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.50, and among those aged 2 to 4 years, where the estimate was 1.86. No significant post-pandemic increase was detected in school-aged children or adolescents, while some estimates could not be calculated because of sparse events. Influenza A increased after reopening in every age group with estimable results except neonates aged 0 to 28 days. Its largest post-pandemic estimate occurred among children aged 5 to 9 years, at 1.74, followed by 1.42 among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years. Discover more Bioengineering Research Papers Learn Engineering Track Biotech Influenza B followed an unusual split between younger and older children. Positivity remained below baseline after reopening among children aged 29 days to 23 months and 2 to 4 years, with adjusted odds ratios of 0.53 and 0.58, respectively. In contrast, it increased among children aged 5 to 9 years, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.21, and rose more strongly among adolescents aged 10 to 17 years, reaching 2.88. The difference between the overall and age-specific results was significant for all four principal pathogens, with age-period interaction P values below 0.001. M. pneumoniae showed a delayed increase concentrated in school-aged children: its post-pandemic adjusted odds ratio was 3.32 at ages 5 to 9 and 1.74 at ages 2 to 4, with no significant increase among infants or adolescents. Outpatient and inpatient sensitivity analyses indicated that care setting also shaped the apparent recovery in some pathogens. Influenza A was elevated overall during Pandemic-II, but its adjusted odds ratio in inpatients was 0.64, suggesting that the early rebound was driven primarily by outpatient testing. Influenza B remained suppressed among inpatients, including an adjusted odds ratio of 0.15 after reopening, while its strong post-pandemic increase among adolescents suggested that the adolescent resurgence was concentrated in outpatient care. Because inpatient testing was used as a proxy for more consistent clinical indications, and because testing indications were not systematically recorded, the authors cautioned that residual confounding could remain even after adjustment and restriction. Discover more Bioengineering Job Board Research Assistant Listings iGEM Team Directory Bioengineering Events Calendar Bioengineer Blog Access Common bacterial culture results followed a different and more uncertain pattern from the viral findings. Staphylococcus aureus positivity increased from 2.7% before the pandemic to 4.2% during Pandemic-I and remained at 3.6% after reopening; its adjusted odds ratios were elevated in all three later periods. Escherichia coli also had elevated adjusted odds across the later periods, while Streptococcus pneumoniae declined after reopening, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.77, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa reached 0.61. These estimates remain difficult to interpret because the composition of cultures changed markedly. Upper-respiratory specimens rose from 91.9% before the pandemic to 99.2% after reopening, while lower-respiratory specimens had much higher culture yields. Hospitalization rates, prior antibiotic exposure, specimen quality and reasons for obtaining cultures also varied, and some bacterial effect estimates reversed when specimen type was included in the model. Co-infection patterns shifted as the dominant pathogens changed. During Pandemic-I, bacterial-bacterial combinations represented 49.0% of co-infections in the study’s main analysis, a period when viral positivity was at its lowest. In a sensitivity analysis excluding dual influenza A and B antigen results, bacterial-bacterial combinations declined from 62.0% during Pandemic-I to 11.2% after reopening, while bacterial-influenza combinations increased substantially and reached 22.9% after reopening. Influenza A-B dual antigen positivity accounted for 49.7% of all co-infections overall and was particularly common among children aged 5 to 9 years and adolescents, but the investigators warned that cross-reactivity in rapid antigen testing could inflate this category. Cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus detections also required caution because they may represent reactivation rather than acute respiratory infection. The study supports an interpretation of disruption followed by non-uniform recovery, not a simple return to the old epidemiological baseline. It also cannot establish the cause of the changes. An immune gap, altered transmission, shifts in social mixing and changing patterns of healthcare use are plausible explanations discussed by the authors, but no serological or immunological measurements were collected, so the immune-gap mechanism remains a hypothesis. Other limitations include the retrospective design, restriction to two referral hospitals in one city, changing test denominators, lower sensitivity of rapid antigen assays for influenza, sparse data in some age-specific strata and differences in period lengths that prevented a strict interrupted time-series analysis. The investigators concluded that the divergent results support consideration of pathogen- and age-specific surveillance, while describing the findings as observations among tested children rather than direct measures of population incidence or evidence that any prevention strategy would prevent infection. Advertisement: 0:11 RSV warning signs: Oklahoma mom says don’t ignore a cough A 4-year-old with Marfan syndrome has been hospitalized for RSV three times this year, and OU Health doctors say prevention is the best protection. OKALHOMA - Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is back in season, and the mother of a 4-year-old girl hospitalized with the virus is sharing the warning signs she wishes she had caught sooner. A cough that turned serious in days Marissa Deitrich said her daughter, Paisley, has been hospitalized with RSV three times this year. Each stay required oxygen. Deitrich decided to speak out about the illness because of what her family has been through. “She is a ball of energy. Nonstop. She’ll talk your ear off. She’s super outgoing.” Deitrich said. Paisley has Marfan syndrome, a condition that makes her more vulnerable to severe illness when respiratory virus season arrives. “This is her third time this year having RSV, and she’s had to be hospitalized for oxygen all three times,” Deitrich said. Deitrich urged parents to watch their children’s symptoms closely. “Even if it’s just a little cough, take it seriously because it can turn into something worse. She had a cough on Monday, a little on Tuesday, and then she was hospitalized on Wednesday,” she said. She said she hopes Paisley will be out of the hospital in a few days. Why RSV can be dangerous OU Health told News 9 that RSV can be devastating for people with weakened immune systems, older adults and newborns. Many people think of RSV as the common cold, and for most healthy people that is accurate, said Dr. Donna Tyungu, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at OU Health. “After about 6 or 7 months of age, as long as someone doesn’t have congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease, it really is the common cold for a general healthy individual,” Tyungu said. Prevention options No specific treatment exists for RSV, so doctors focus on prevention. “The only management that we really have for RSV at this point in time is prevention,” Tyungu said. Women who are 32 to 36 weeks pregnant can get a vaccine that passes RSV antibodies to the baby before the respiratory virus season, according to OU Health. Tyungu recommended that mothers who are interested contact their providers. Doctors also offer RSV monoclonal antibody injections to infants to protect against severe illness. OU Health encouraged families to talk with their health care providers about protection. Elizabeth Fitz Elizabeth Fitz joined the News 9 team in October 2024. She is passionate about investigative stories and also enjoys reporting on education and public safety. Elizabeth cares deeply about telling stories that give voices to marginalized communities and make positive impacts. Children's Health Health insurers balk at paying for newborns' RSV immunization in the hospital October 16, 20264:46 PM ET Heard on All Things Considered Rob Stein Health insurers balk at paying for newborns' RSV immunization in the hospital Listen · 3:44 3:44 Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5985001/nx-s1-9967506" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript Many infants are leaving the hospital without getting immunized against RSV. Why? Because many insurance companies won't pay for the shots while the newborn is in the hospital. Transcript SCOTT DETROW, HOST: There are powerful new ways to protect newborn babies against a dangerous respiratory virus known as RSV, yet many infants are still being left vulnerable. NPR health correspondent Rob Stein explains why. ROB STEIN, BYLINE: For decades, doctors and parents were helpless against RSV. The respiratory syncytial virus sent tens of thousands of newborns to the hospital each year, where they often fought for their lives in intensive care. JESSE HACKELL: Those kids can go from mildly ill to deathly ill in a matter of hours, and I've seen that happen. STEIN: Dr. Jesse Hackell is with the American Academy of Pediatrics. HACKELL: These can be very, very sick infants, and it is just something I just never want to see. There's no reason to see it. STEIN: Because three years ago, doctors finally got ways to protect babies against RSV, a vaccine for pregnant women so they can pass protective antibodies to their babies in the womb and shots of laboratory-made antibodies that shield newborns whose mothers didn't get vaccinated. HACKELL: It's been a game-changer. We have seen a tremendous decrease in the amount of both RSV illness, and there's been a huge reduction, over 60%, I believe, in the rate of hospitalization for RSV disease. And that's just massive. STEIN: But Hackell and others say far too many babies are still catching RSV. HACKELL: Only about 40% of eligible pregnant people received the vaccine during pregnancy. So that means that 60% of babies are being born without any protection. Of those 60% of babies, 40% of eligible babies were not getting protected, and that's pretty big. STEIN: RSV is still among the most common reasons babies end up in the hospital. Now, there are several reasons for this, but the big one is that many hospitals don't routinely offer the antibody shots for RSV to newborns before they get discharged. Dr. Michelle Fiscus is a pediatrician who serves as the chief medical officer for the Association of Immunization Managers. MICHELLE FISCUS: The best way to protect them is to immunize them within the first seven days of life, preferably before they ever leave the hospital after being born, because as soon as they leave, they are exposed to that virus during respiratory season. STEIN: But most insurance companies aren't reimbursing hospitals for giving the shots, which cost about $500 each. That's because hospitals typically negotiate bundled insurance payments for everything they do to deliver and care for babies, and not all babies need the shots because their moms got vaccinated or the babies aren't born during RSV season. Parents can get their babies immunized for free from a doctor's office, but Fiscus says many don't get the shot there in time. FISCUS: There's a sizable proportion of babies that do not make it to their first checkup within the first seven days of life when they're supposed to be receiving these products. And so this barrier on the commercial insurance side is causing babies to be left vulnerable. STEIN: Hospitals could offer more kids shots, say, by signing up for a federal program that provides immunizations for free. But the American Hospital Association says that program doesn't really solve the insurance nag. In a statement to NPR, the group representing commercial insurance companies, American's Health Insurance Plans (ph), says they are fully committed to providing RSV protection to babies, but they are not required to pay for the immunizations in the hospital, only in doctors' offices. supplementary_news.content_title: 基于宏基因组二代测序解析喀麦隆国家流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子的呼吸道病原谱 - 生物通
supplementary_news.content: 基于宏基因组二代测序解析喀麦隆国家流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子的呼吸道病原谱 《Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses》:Use of Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing to Investigate Respiratory Pathogens in Influenza-Negative Nasopharyngeal Swabs From Cameroon's National Influenza Surveillance 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月21日 来源:Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses 3.9 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Open Access 背景:在喀麦隆,国家流感监测可识别流感阳性病例,但非流感急性呼吸道感染(ARIs)的病因仍缺乏充分表征。研究人员应用宏基因组二代测序(mNGS)调查通过国家流感监测采集的流感阴性鼻咽拭子中的呼吸道病原体。 方法:研究人员分析了2023年9月至12月期间从流感样疾病(ILI)或严重急性呼吸道感染(SARI)患者中采集的199份流感阴性鼻咽拭子。制备混合DNA/RNA文库并在Illumina NovaSeq平台测序。使用METAMIC(v2.0)和SPAdes(V3.15.5)生物信息学流程进行分类学鉴定。 结果:在120/199份样本(60.3%,95% CI: 53.5%, 67.1%)中检出病毒序列,代表15种病毒。最常见病毒为鼻病毒(rhinovirus,43/131)、呼吸道合胞病毒(respiratory syncytial virus, RSV,33/131)、流感病毒(influenza virus)、副流感病毒(parainfluenza virus)和肠道病毒(enterovirus)。还检出两种非呼吸道病毒(Rotavirus和Papillomavirus)。测序平均每份样本产生2610万条读段(reads),每份样本平均深度870.3,平均基因组覆盖度(genomic coverage)82%。鉴定出11例病毒合并感染(co-infections)。还检出若干细菌和真菌属(bacterial and fungal genera)。 结论:该研究表明,mNGS为表征喀麦隆呼吸道病原体提供了强大且无偏倚(unbiased)的方法,揭示流感阴性ARI病例中存在显著病毒多样性。然而,成本和生物信息学能力仍是常规实施(routine implementation)的主要障碍。需要纵向研究(longitudinal studies)和临床相关性分析,以加强解释并指导将mNGS整合入国家监测。 论文主体解读:急性呼吸道感染(acute respiratory infections, ARIs)是全球感染性疾病相关发病和死亡的主要原因,临床范围可从普通感冒等自限性疾病到肺炎和急性呼吸窘迫综合征等严重疾病,病原包括病毒、细菌、真菌和寄生虫。喀麦隆约24%的ARI患者需要住院;在低中等收入国家(low- and middle-income countries, LMICs),可靠分子诊断工具可及性有限,ARI病因认识仍存在明显缺口。当前诊断主要依赖PCR(polymerase chain reaction),该类方法依赖已知病毒序列,难以识别意外或新发病原。喀麦隆自2007年开展流感监测,Centre Pasteur du Cameroun(CPC)为国家流感中心,每年从哨点采集约1000份呼吸道疾病患者样本,10年研究显示年阳性率为24%—29%,COVID-19扰乱了流感季节性并降低检出率。多年监测后,非流感ARI病因信息仍有限,既往研究主要依赖靶向PCR,可能漏检新发、再发、罕见或高度特异病原。因此,研究人员应用mNGS对喀麦隆流感监测中流感阴性鼻咽拭子进行呼吸道病原全面调查。该研究首次在喀麦隆应用mNGS调查流感阴性ARI病例呼吸道病原,揭示显著病毒多样性,显示mNGS作为无偏倚诊断工具的潜力,同时指出成本和生物信息学能力限制其常规应用,并建议多重呼吸道panel和纵向研究。 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 领 取 方法概括(不超过250字):研究人员开展横断面研究,样本来自2023年9—12月喀麦隆国家流感监测哨点(7/10行政区)的流感阴性鼻咽拭子,患者符合ILI或SARI定义;最终对199份样本进行mNGS(150份ILI、49份SARI)。湿实验室采用机械破坏、酶消化和化学裂解提取总核酸,构建DNA/RNA文库,在Illumina NovaSeq 6000测序。干实验室使用MetaMIC v2.0和SPAdes v3.15.5流程,剔除人源及非病原序列,以>10 million reads和1E-5病原读段比例阈值判定,并设环境样本和ZymoBIOMICS标准品质控。病毒阳性样本进一步组装、共识序列构建、分型及系统发育分析。 3.1 研究人群的一般特征:通过横断面mNGS分析,199份鼻咽拭子成功检测,包括150份ILI和49份SARI,采集于2023年9—12月,来自喀麦隆10个行政区中的7个;研究人群含104名女性和95名男性,年龄0—80岁,平均14.1岁;4份样本未达到10 M阈值,被判为不可解释并排除。 3.2 病毒检测与遗传多样性:通过宏基因组测序、基因组组装和系统发育分析,全部鼻咽拭子平均产生2610万条reads,平均41%来自人基因组、43%来自细菌、3%来自真菌、1%来自病毒,其余12%来自未显著匹配已知数据库的其他病毒和非病原类群。病毒reads平均测序深度为870.3,120/199份样本(60.3%,95% CI: 53.5%, 67.1%)检出病毒;组装后病毒基因组平均覆盖度为82%(5%—100%)。共鉴定11例病毒合并感染,获得131条病毒序列,包括Rhinovirus(43/131)、RSV(33/131)、Influenza virus(14/131)、Parainfluenza virus(13/131)、Enterovirus(11/131)、Adenovirus(4/131)、Cytomegalovirus(3/131)、Metapneumovirus(2/131)、Polyomavirus(2/131)、SARS-CoV-2(1/131)、Torque teno virus(1/131)、Human Coronavirus HKU1(1/131)和Epstein–Barr virus(1/131);另在2例患者中检出Rotavirus和Papillomavirus两种非呼吸道病毒。92.4%(121/131)的病毒株属于Rhinovirus、RSV、Influenza virus、Parainfluenza virus和Enterovirus五类主要呼吸道病毒。系统发育分析显示Rhinovirus遗传变异显著,鉴定23个不同亚型,分属Enterovirus alpharhino(RV-A)、Enterovirus betarhino(RV-B)和Enterovirus cerhino(RV-C);Enterovirus strains分为Enterovirus alphacoxsackie(EV-A)、Enterovirus betacoxsackie(EV-B)和Enterovirus coxsackiepol(EV-C)三血清型;Influenza strains包括5株Influenza A virus、4株Influenza B virus和5株Influenza C virus;RSV序列聚为RSV-A和RSV-B两型,以A型为主;Parainfluenza virus对应Human orthorubulavirus 4和Human respirovirus 1;其余病毒多样性较低,序列聚为单一型。 3.3 细菌和真菌检测:通过mNGS分类分析,平均43%和3%的reads分别来自细菌和真菌;细菌和真菌分别在61份和21份/199份鼻咽拭子中检出。检出的细菌包括Chlamydia pneumoniae、Corynebacterium(propinquum、efficiens、urealyticum、yudongzhengii、pseudodiphtheriticum、doosanense等)、Enterobacter hormaechei、Haemophilus(influenzae、aegyptius、haemolyticus、seminalis、caudoviricetes sp.、haemolyticus)、Klebsiella pneumoniae、Moraxella(catarrhalis、nonliquefaciens、osloensis)、Staphylococcus(aureus、epidermidis)、Streptococcus(oralis、pneumoniae、pyogenes、mitis)和Actinomyces(oris、naeslundii);真菌包括Candida(parapsilosis、metapsilosis、orthopsilosis、auris)。 A和B在先前阴性样本中检出更值得关注。比较mNGS与常规PCR监测的研究报道两法存在差异,但未证明mNGS敏感性更优;整合mNGS与常规PCR可更准确表征资源有限地区呼吸道感染。研究意外检出Rotavirus和Papillomavirus,为喀麦隆呼吸道样本首次报告,但其与临床症状的关联尚不明确,需进一步确认是否为真正呼吸道病原或污染。细菌和真菌reads比例高,原文认为可由环境污染DNA或无症状定植解释;Polyomavirus、CMV、Actinomyces oris、Moraxella catarrhalis、Corynebacterium spp.、Haemophilus influenzae、Candida parapsilosis和C. pseudohaemulonis等通常属于正常口咽 panels),其已覆盖本研究所鉴定几乎所有病毒且已商业化。此外,需要纵向研究以捕捉呼吸道病原传播的季节性变化及mNGS发现的临床解释。 论文主体解读:急性呼吸道感染(acute respiratory infections, chain reaction),该类方法依赖已知病毒序列,难以识别意外或新发病原。喀麦隆自2007年开展流感监测,Centre Pasteur du
